transcript:
# Day 23, Game Theory and Decisions: Chicken and the stag hunt, risk versus trust (Rousseau, 1755; Chicken formalized in the 1950s)

Two teams at your bank both want the same budget line for next year. Each can hold firm or back down. If both hold firm, the request stalls, the executive sponsor gets annoyed, and both lose. If one backs down, the other wins. If both back down, you split it awkwardly and nobody is happy, but nobody is hurt. Now a second situation. Two partner banks could build a shared fraud platform. If both commit, each gets something far better than going alone. If one commits and the other quietly keeps its old system, the committed one has spent money for nothing. Going alone is safe but mediocre.

These are two of the most useful games in the whole subject, and they feel similar from the inside. Both are two player games with two choices. Both have a cooperative outcome that is hard to reach. But they fail for opposite reasons, and telling them apart changes what you should do.

The first is Chicken. The name comes from the 1950s image of two drivers racing toward each other; whoever swerves first is the chicken. The key feature is that the worst outcome is mutual stubbornness. Each player wants to hold firm only if the other swerves. Game theory calls a stable pair of choices a Nash equilibrium, meaning neither player can do better by changing alone. Chicken has two of them: you swerve and I hold, or I swerve and you hold. Neither player wants to be the one who gives, and that is the whole drama. The game rewards whoever can make the other believe they will not swerve. This is why budget fights, labor negotiations, and standoffs between nations so often involve public statements that tie your own hands. The crazy looking move is sometimes the strongest one.

The second is the stag hunt. Jean-Jacques Rousseau described it in his Discourse on Inequality in 1755. Two hunters can each hunt a stag, which only works if both stay on the stag, or each can wander off after a rabbit, which always works but gives much less. The key feature here is that mutual cooperation is the best outcome for everyone. Nobody is tempted to cheat if they are sure the other will cooperate. The problem is not greed; it is doubt. Game theorists say the stag outcome is payoff dominant (best for all) while the rabbit outcome is risk dominant (safest if you are unsure). The shared fraud platform is a stag hunt. Nobody wants to defect. They just want to be sure the other one will show up.

So Chicken is a game about risk and nerve, and the stag hunt is a game about trust and assurance. In Chicken, communication can make things worse, because each side uses it to signal toughness. In the stag hunt, communication is nearly the whole solution. A credible promise, a visible first step, a contract with penalties, or just a track record can move everyone to the stag.

The strongest objection is that real situations rarely come with their payoffs printed on them. Experiments by economists like Russell Cooper and others in the 1990s found that people often choose the rabbit even when the stag is clearly better, and small changes in how the game is described shift behavior a lot. Critics say this makes the models descriptive labels rather than predictions. Defenders answer that the labels still do real work: once you decide whether you are in Chicken or a stag hunt, you know whether the problem is nerve or assurance, and that tells you what to fix.

This builds on last week's coordination games and focal points. The stag hunt is a coordination game with a twist: one meeting point is better but scarier. Chicken links to the Strategy track, where Schelling will later show how burning your bridges can win a game of nerve, and to Sun Tzu's idea that the skilled general shapes the ground so the enemy backs down before fighting.

Question for the day: pick one standoff you are in right now. Is it Chicken, where someone must give, or a stag hunt, where nobody wants to defect and you just need assurance? Would you act differently once you name it?

Optional source: Rousseau, Discourse on the Origin of Inequality (1755), Part Two, the passage on the hunters and the deer, a few short paragraphs.
